questions.q: What is a physical change?
questions.a: A change in shape, size or state where no new substance forms and the change can usually be reversed.

questions.q: Give two examples of physical changes.
questions.a: Melting of ice and tearing of paper (also dissolving sugar).

questions.q: Is dissolving salt in water reversible? How?
questions.a: Yes - evaporating the water leaves the salt back, unchanged.

questions.q: What is a chemical change?
questions.a: A change in which new substances with new properties form, usually not reversible - like rusting of iron.

questions.q: Give two examples of chemical changes.
questions.a: Burning of paper and curdling of milk (also rusting).

questions.q: How can you tell a chemical change has occurred?
questions.a: A new substance forms, often with colour change, gas, heat or light - and it cannot be undone simply.

questions.q: What happens when magnesium ribbon burns in air?
questions.a: It burns with dazzling white light forming white magnesium oxide powder - a chemical change.

questions.q: Why must magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning?
questions.a: A coating of magnesium oxide blocks the metal; rubbing exposes fresh magnesium to burn.

questions.q: Is burning of magnesium reversible?
questions.a: No - a new substance (MgO) forms, so it is a chemical change.

questions.q: What happens when an iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution?
questions.a: Iron displaces copper: the blue colour fades and a brown copper coating forms on the nail.

questions.q: Why is the copper sulphate reaction called a displacement reaction?
questions.a: The more reactive iron pushes copper out of its salt solution.

questions.q: Is the copper sulphate-iron reaction chemical or physical? Why?
questions.a: Chemical - new substances (iron sulphate, copper) form with new properties.

questions.q: How do we test for carbon dioxide gas?
questions.a: Bubble it through lime water - the limewater turns milky due to calcium carbonate.

questions.q: Why does lime water turn milky with CO2?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide reacts with clear calcium hydroxide to form insoluble white calcium carbonate.

questions.q: What happens if excess CO2 passes through the milky limewater?
questions.a: The milkiness clears as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms.

questions.q: What is rusting? Write the conditions needed for it.
questions.a: Iron combining with oxygen and water to form brown rust (iron oxide) - both air and moisture are needed.

questions.q: What kind of change is rusting?
questions.a: A chemical change - new substance (rust) forms and cannot be reversed to iron.

questions.q: Why does an iron pan rust faster in the rainy season?
questions.a: Moisture in air is high, and water plus oxygen speed up rusting.

questions.q: Give three ways to prevent rusting.
questions.a: Painting or greasing the surface, galvanising with zinc, and keeping iron dry.

questions.q: Why does a galvanised iron sheet not rust even if scratched?
questions.a: Zinc coats the iron and zinc itself corrodes very slowly, protecting the exposed edge too.

questions.q: How does oiling protect machine parts?
questions.a: The oil film keeps air and moisture away from the metal surface.

questions.q: What is crystallisation?
questions.a: Separating pure solid crystals of a substance from its solution by cooling or evaporation.

questions.q: Why is crystallisation better than simple evaporation for obtaining salt?
questions.a: It gives pure, well-shaped crystals, while evaporation may leave impurities and burn the substance.

questions.q: Name one substance obtained by crystallisation in daily life.
questions.a: Sugar crystals (or alum, copper sulphate crystals).
